Senses.Explanation: The discriminating mind is the mind described as raising divisions among encountered things, positions, or qualities; Chan records define, criticize, and contrast this operation. The Mirror Record says that when discrimination arises, perceived objects appear, and calls that arising ignorance. Huanyou Chuan says a discriminating mind starts when people take what appears before them as outside their own share. Baizhang Huaihai's exchange asks how an undivided knowing could cut the mind that sees and discriminates, then continues until both sword and knowing are unavailable. Other records contrast discriminating and undiscriminating minds without turning the latter into a prescribed exercise.

Senses.Explanation: The moon is plainly on the plum blossom; by the time you look at the blossom, you are already late. Warn that turning to inspect an obvious sign can miss the immediate occasion. Eryin Mi and Baiyu Jingsi use the complete saying in distinct recorded teaching turns. Yikui Yuankui, Feiyin Tongrong, and Shiyu Mingfang give further current deployments. The image turns on timing and attention, not a claim that the moon rests physically on a blossom.

Senses.Explanation: A fixing seal — take clear note of this — ruled at the root over Nanquan's sifter-question and stamped across first halls, graph-corrections, birthday seats, and farewells from the Song openings to the Qing exchanges. The root sits in Nanquan Puyuan's own answer, carried in the imperially selected record: he asks the arriving monk where he comes from — from sifting flour — hand or foot? and at the silence: you ask me, and I will tell you; asked as told, the seal: take clear note of this; later, meeting a clear-eyed man, raise it to him; Foyan Qingyuan, opening his first hall at Tianning of Shuzhou, receives the installation document from the circuit scholar-official, shows the assembly — heaven cannot cover it, earth cannot bear it, the heaven-leaking secret divulged, every word worth loving — and what is the worth-loving word?; a long stillness, then: take clear note of this, raise it to a maker — and the document passed on to the announcer; Gaofeng Yuanmiao, in the gathered appraisals of Mazu's four strokes — one long above, three short below; say neither long nor short; answer me beyond the strokes — with Mazu's single line drawn on the ground, no long or short, answered — rules the copies themselves: a character thrice copied turns crow into horse; Xifeng cannot hold the laugh and corrects it for you all; a long while, then calling the attendant: take clear note of this; and Chushi Fanqi, at the sentient-and-insentient swap — mountains, rivers, and earth, bamboo ends and wood chips all sentient; the buddhas and bodhisattvas, beasts and donkeys all insentient — calls the assembly: why did the insentient turn sentient, the sentient turn insentient?; take clear note of this, raise it to a maker. Guantao Daqi, after the discourse that ran the thousand buddhas of the past — cause-ground and fruit-ocean, the ease and hardship of their teaching, lifespans long and short, prophecies many and few — through the thousand of the present and the thousand to come, whose vows and attainments have no end, ends on the staff's own rejoicing verse — a countenance of wonder, light filling the ten directions; once I made offering, and now again draw near — and suddenly calls the assembly: take clear note of this; Miaoyun Zhenxiong, taking leave of the hall, gathers going and staying into one freedom — sometimes the treasure-mirror deep-hidden, beauty and ugliness never stood; sometimes the flower-treasury flung open, light filling the whole realm; the rabbit-horn staff fierce as a tiger, every stroke beyond pattern, the head out past heaven itself — and over the old saying — where there is a buddha, do not stay; where there is no buddha, hurry past — does anyone in the assembly get it?; the staff strikes: three thousand li away, take clear note of this; and Feiyin Tongrong, at the prefect Wei's birthday seat in the magistrate's office, trades couplets with the asking monk — falling sunset and lone duck fly together; autumn water and the long sky one color; one man has his blessing and all people lean on it — and seals the exchange: take clear note of this.

Entries.SourceTerm: 分明香在梅花上，尋到梅花香又無

Senses.PreferredTarget: The fragrance is plainly on the plum blossom, yet when you search the blossom the fragrance is nowhere to be found.
SearchAliases: plum blossom fragrance disappears when sought
Senses.Note: The image turns on something present and perceptible that cannot be grasped as an object. The sources do not deny that flowers have scent; the failed search is the teaching turn.

Senses.Explanation: The fragrance is plainly on the plum blossom, yet when you search the blossom the fragrance is nowhere to be found. The image turns on something present and perceptible that cannot be grasped as an object. Senses.Explanation: Unable to account for it or sort it out. The phrase has 107 exact occurrences in 66 source files representing 66 works. An unnamed questioner says he cannot account for a distinction between expounding teachings and responding to the occasion; Yuan’an Feng tells another questioner, ‘Look at you, unable to account for it’; and Yuan’an, Linye Tongqi, and Linye Tongqi’s later lamp-record version use it of their own inability to settle a fan-name test, a north-or-south salutation, or which recorded saying is deep or shallow. Zhaozhou Congshen’s ‘the highest way is not difficult’ exchange supplies a famous duration formula: he says someone once asked him and he was unable to account for it for five years. Yuan’an’s later letter turns the verb back on the reader: if unable to account for it, one must carefully account for it.

Senses.Explanation: A coordinate pair naming “principle” and “affairs, events, or matters.” Chan records ask how principle and affairs are unobstructed, say that both sides have been penetrated or are fully provided, and require them to be clearly distinguished. The Mirror Record gives one explicit account of their relation: “This principle is the principle that completes affairs; this affair is the affair that displays principle.” Ying’an says, “Penetrated on the side of principle and penetrated on the side of affairs: this is called principle and affairs fused through.” Other records speak of both being complete or ask directly, “What are principle and affairs?” The expression is translated as the coordinate pair stated by the texts rather than collapsed into one abstract category.

Xueguan Zhixun contrasts downstream pushing with steering against wind; Sanshan Lai calls the easy move incomplete; Aziwa uses it for complying with a request; Wansong Xingxiu and Langshan Yu make critical appraisals; Yinyuan Longqi contrasts it with sailing on land and raising waves on a mountain.

Senses.PreferredTarget: when a poison-bird feather falls into the water, fish and turtles die
AlternateTargets: a zhen-bird feather drops into water and kills fish and turtles

Senses.Note: The zhen is the poisonous bird whose feather carries the image’s lethal force; the occurrence is proverbial, not a zoological claim about an ordinary bird.

Occurrences.Kwic: 堂。世尊初生下時。分手指天地道。天上天下惟我獨尊。也是半夜拾得錫。後來雲門大師道。我當時若見。一棒打殺。與狗子喫。貴圖天下太平。獻佛不假香多。南山今日。要與黃面老子出氣。卓主丈云。鴆羽落水魚鼈死。結夏上堂。拈主丈云。主丈子。久靜思動。欲出來發揮古佛二千年前底嚴規。要驗納僧九十日之功用。左顧右盻。朝誦夕思。直教入林不動草入水不動波。以表行脚從人之德。卓主丈云。主丈子。爾從上

Senses.Explanation: Xutang Zhiyu strikes his staff and says that a poison-bird feather dropped into water kills the fish and turtles. The line follows Xutang’s retelling of the newborn Buddha’s claim and Yunmen’s wish to strike him dead. Xutang says that today he will give the old yellow-faced one an outlet, then supplies the lethal-water image.
